item.title: Alamogordo Tigers Dominate Chaparral 54-0 in 5A First Round, Advance to Face Los Lunas
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — The Alamogordo Tigers made a statement in the opening round of the 2026 Nusenda Credit Union 5A Football Championships, rolling past the No. 12 Chaparral Lobos 54-0 on Friday night at Tiger Stadium. The win improves Alamogordo to 7-4 and sends the fifth-seeded Tigers into the quarterfinals against the No. 4 Los Lunas Tigers.

Alamogordo’s offense clicked from the start in a dominant performance that featured a balanced attack and multiple big plays. Scoring unfolded as follows, according to live updates from Otero County Sports:

• Qymani Patterson scored on a 45-yard TD run (Russell extra point good) for a 7-0 lead.

• Nathanael Cereceres added a 9-yard TD run (Russell XP no good), making it 13-0 at the end of the first quarter.

• Tristan Bowman ran it in from 9 yards (Bowman 2-point conversion run good) to push the lead to 21-0 early in the second.

• Cereceres connected with Rudy Wolfe on an 18-yard TD pass (Russell XP good) for 28-0.

• Cereceres then hit Bowman on a 76-yard TD strike (Russell XP good), giving the Tigers a 35-0 halftime lead.

• Leyton Niland scored from 2 yards in the third (Russell XP no good) to make it 41-0.

• Rudy Wolfe broke a 51-yard TD run (XP good) for 48-0.

• Niland closed the scoring with a 42-yard TD run for the final 54-0.

MaxPreps reported Alamogordo piled up 351 rushing yards and 150 passing yards. Cereceres was efficient through the air (5-of-7 for 141 yards and two TDs), Patterson led the ground game with 110 yards and a score on seven carries, and Bowman hauled in 111 receiving yards with a touchdown. The Tigers had scored 54 unanswered points after previously beating Chaparral 56-7 in the regular-season finale.

The shutout marked a strong home performance for a team that earned the No. 5 seed after a solid finish to the regular season. Alamogordo will now travel to Los Lunas for a quarterfinal matchup set for Saturday, November 14, at 1 p.m.

Rest of the 5A First Round and Quarterfinal Picture

The first round wrapped up over the weekend with several decisive results:

• No. 8 Santa Fe defeated No. 9 Cibola 23-7 in Santa Fe. It was the Demons’ first home playoff game in 41 years.

• No. 6 Gadsden blanked No. 11 Mayfield 50-0.

• No. 7 Goddard edged No. 10 Highland 35-22.

Top seeds Roswell, Piedra Vista, Artesia, and Los Lunas all received first-round byes. The quarterfinals are scheduled for November 13-14:

• No. 1 Roswell vs. No. 8 Santa Fe (Friday, Nov. 13 at 6 p.m.)

• No. 4 Los Lunas vs. No. 5 Alamogordo (Saturday, Nov. 14 at 1 p.m. in Los Lunas)

• No. 3 Artesia vs. No. 6 Gadsden (Saturday, Nov. 14 at 1 p.m.)

• No. 2 Piedra Vista vs. No. 7 Goddard (Saturday, Nov. 14 at 1 p.m.)

Semifinals are set for November 20-21, with the 5A championship scheduled for November 28. Los Lunas enters the quarterfinals as a dangerous No. 4 seed with a strong regular-season resume and recent wins that included a 50-0 victory over Highland.

For Alamogordo, the focus now shifts to preparation for a road test against a Los Lunas team that also features a physical style of play. The Tigers showed explosive capability in the first round and will look to carry that momentum into the next round of the Nusenda Credit Union 5A Football Championships.

Chris Edwards is the publisher of Alamogordo Town News and a longtime local sports and community reporter and author of several books on Alamogordo sports history.

item.title: Disagreement Isn’t Disloyalty
item.description:
Guest Editorial

By Dr. Stephanie Hernandez

Now that the election is over, I find myself reflecting on the part of politics I dislike most: how quickly disagreement becomes permission to tear people down.

During a social media exchange, I said I hated politics. The former chair of the Republican Party of New Mexico responded that it was a good thing because I wasn’t good at it. I believe that was intended as an insult, but it wasn’t. If being good at politics means insulting people who think for themselves, I can live with that assessment.

That exchange reflects a larger problem: treating shared party affiliation as an obligation to fall in line. Shared principles should leave room to question behavior and should never require surrendering independent judgment.

My upbringing and faith taught me to treat people with respect and let my work speak for itself. Public service taught me that accountability sometimes requires difficult conversations. We can question decisions and challenge conduct without resorting to degrading behavior.

Anyone who knows my fiscal conservatism won’t be surprised that I’m a Republican. I support the Second Amendment, lower taxes, a strong military, personal responsibility, and accountable government. I can hold those convictions and still cringe at something my own party says or does.

I registered Republican in 1995, at eighteen, the first in my family to do so. I came from hardworking, blue-collar Democrats who valued earning their way and taking care of their families, and I remain proud of that heritage. But I believed in a strong military and fiscal responsibility at a time when the Clinton administration was shrinking the military and civilian defense workforce after the Cold War. I couldn’t get behind that direction. Choosing a different party did not mean rejecting the values my family taught me.

Years later, I met my husband while he was working on my cousin’s campaign as a Democrat. Our conversations helped him recognize that his conservative beliefs, military background, and Christian faith aligned more closely with the Republican Party. Political affiliation should develop through thought and conversation.

My friends and family hold views across the political spectrum. I don’t vote a straight ticket. A party label gets a candidate my attention, not my vote. I consider candidates’ qualifications and look for common ground, even with people I don’t fully agree with.

Although my husband was deeply involved in politics throughout our marriage, I largely stayed away from any involvement. When I was city manager, former Mayor Susan Payne helped me recognize that my lack of knowledge about Alamogordo’s political history was affecting my ability to do my job. Like it or not, a city manager must understand the political environment well enough to navigate it while serving the community.

Susan and I were not close before 2023. We were still getting to know each other when tragedy brought us together as mayor and city manager after one of our officers was killed in the line of duty.

Over five difficult days, we found our rhythm. We both spent time with the family and supported our officers while carrying out different primary responsibilities. As mayor and a mother, Susan provided a comforting public presence. As city manager, I coordinated resources, supported our staff, and kept city operations moving. Our roles overlapped, and we trusted each other to recognize where we were needed.

That experience became the foundation of our friendship, and other challenges that year strengthened it. She helped me understand the history behind political relationships I had underestimated, and I came to appreciate why simply doing good work did not make me immune to politics. Our friendship never meant we agreed on everything. It meant we had learned to trust each other through difficult work.

As our friendship grew, I believe some Republican leaders and supporters treated our association, and our willingness to question leadership, as disloyalty. Susan and others who spoke against what they believed was wrong faced criticism that, from my perspective, was often harsher than anything I experienced.

This election cycle, I became more involved and openly supported candidates. Beyond my own experience, I saw disputes here in Otero County raised similar questions about party loyalty and accountability. The state party chair also served as a county commissioner. When she drew a Republican primary challenger, a dispute arose over party rules requiring her to vacate the chairmanship. She remained in that position until a judge ordered her to vacate the chairmanship in May. Asking whether party rules apply equally to everyone is a legitimate question of accountability.

The statewide response showed how quickly that argument turned personal. A state senator defended the chair and portrayed Republican critics as more concerned with displaying their power than winning elections. Yet person he was defending, had publicly criticized others for less, casting them as a minority blocking progress. Defending one faction while questioning the motives of another does little to build unity. The same standards should apply to everyone, regardless of whose side they’re on.

There were calls for unity, but the public exchanges told a different story. In May, a Republican candidate questioned the senator’s honesty or understanding of the rules. In October, a candidate for Republican Party chair announced he was leaving the GOP to register as an independent, while making clear he was not abandoning his conservative values. His decision raises a question: how many people will keep their convictions but walk away from their parties?

It doesn’t have to be that way. Researchers who study groups describe dissent as one of the “normal and healthy aspects of group life.” A party willing to examine itself has room to improve. But will the parties reflect on their own conduct, or are they more comfortable letting people walk away than making room for disagreement?

After researching independent voters extensively for a client, I understand the appeal of political independence and the frustration with being expected to defend a party. Disappointment with politics should make us more deliberate with our votes. It should not persuade us to surrender them.

Congratulations to everyone elected to serve. The campaign is over, but the responsibility to earn the public’s trust continues. That includes listening to people who voted differently, respecting disagreement, and working with others for the good of the community.

As citizens, our responsibility continues, too. We should stay informed, participate, and hold those we support to the same standards as those we oppose.

Holding leaders accountable should never be mistaken for disloyalty and blind loyalty should never be expected.

Dr. Stephanie Hernandez is a Republican and former Alamogordo city manager, serving 31 months combined tenure.

item.title: NMSP arrests driver on DWI-related charges following three-vehicle crash that left 11 injured
item.description:
TULAROSA, N.M. — A 24-year-old man is facing DWI-related charges after New Mexico State Police say he ran a stop sign and caused a three-vehicle crash near Tularosa on Friday afternoon that sent 11 people to the hospital, including two who were flown to El Paso.

New Mexico State Police (NMSP) arrested Oren J. Shanta following the crash on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. He has been charged with great bodily harm by vehicle (DWI) and reckless driving.

NMSP officers were dispatched at approximately 4:04 p.m. to the intersection of U.S. 70 and Old Mescalero Road, where a black Chevrolet passenger car, a white van and a silver SUV had collided.

When officers arrived, emergency medical personnel were already treating multiple patients. Fire crews worked to free three people who were trapped inside the van.

According to witness statements, Shanta was driving the Chevrolet northbound on Old Mescalero Road at a high rate of speed when he failed to stop at the stop sign at U.S. 70. His car struck the white van, which was carrying 10 people, and the silver SUV, which was carrying three.

At least six passengers from the van, two passengers from the Chevrolet and Shanta himself were taken to a local hospital for treatment. Two additional passengers from the van were airlifted to a hospital in El Paso.

While speaking with Shanta at the scene, officers reported detecting the odor of alcohol coming from him and observing other signs that led them to believe he was impaired.

After further investigation, officers placed Shanta under arrest. He is charged with:

Great bodily harm by vehicle (DWI)

Reckless driving

No fatalities have been reported. The current conditions of those injured have not been released.

Charges are accusations only. Shanta is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law.

Information in this article was provided by the New Mexico State Police.

item.title: Proposed Pecan Council Changes Could Shrink New Mexico's Voice
item.description:
New Mexico grew about a third of the nation's pecans in 2024, but a federal proposal published Monday would remove the state's guaranteed seats for pecan shellers on the board that runs the industry's marketing order.

The Trump Administration’s U.S. Department of Agriculture's Department proposed rule (91 FR 70809, Docket AMS-SC-25-0881) would merge the American Pecan Council's three regional sheller districts into one national district. It would also require monthly reports on pecans traded between handlers and add penalties for late assessment payments.

Growers, shellers and buyers in Doña Ana, Chaves, Luna, Otero, Sierra and Lea counties have until Dec. 9, 2026, to comment.

The Council voted 14–0 on Aug. 14, 2025, to recommend the changes, according to the proposal. USDA says the number of shellers has dropped from 50 in 2016 to fewer than 30 as of August 2025, leaving sheller seats hard to fill.

One national sheller region. Today, the Eastern, Central and Western regions each get two sheller seats: one for a sheller handling more than 12.5 million pounds a year and one for a smaller sheller. The proposal opens all six seats to any qualified sheller, regardless of location or size. Staggered two- and four-year terms would follow.

Monthly transfer reports. Handlers who pass pecans to another handler would report each month instead of once a season. The report would add the weight and type of inshell pecans moved. USDA notes transfers usually run November through February.

Late-payment penalties. Assessments unpaid 30 days after the due date would draw a one-time 5% charge, plus 1% interest per month on the unpaid balance. On a $1,000 assessment, that is $50 up front, then about $10.50 a month.

The National Pecan Shellers Association supported the sheller change, USDA said.

New Mexico ranked second in the nation in 2024 with 84.8 million pounds, 32% of U.S. production, worth $167.1 million at $1.97 a pound, according to USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service.

Arizona ranked third at 16.5%. Together, the two Western states grew nearly half the U.S. crop.

Under the current rules, the Western region (Arizona, California and New Mexico) is guaranteed two of the Council's six sheller seats.

Under the proposal, it would be guaranteed none. Western shellers would compete in a single nationwide vote of all shellers.

The seats are already hard to fill. In February 2026, USDA's call for nominees listed open small-sheller seats in all three regions, including the West.

The change could cut both ways. Supporters say open seats mean fewer vacancies and more sheller voices at the table. But with no guaranteed Western seat, the region could end up with fewer shellers on the Council than its share of the crop would suggest.

Doña Ana County alone produced 55 million pounds in 2024, about 21% of the national crop, making it the country's largest pecan-producing county, according to NMSU extension economists. Every southern county with published figures is on the list below.

In Otero County, bearing acreage held at 1,700 acres from 2022 through 2024, while output fell from 2.93 million pounds in 2023 to 2.26 million in 2024. Local growers would see no direct change, but buyers and handlers there would face the new monthly transfer reports during harvest season.

NMSU economists estimate every $1 of pecan output generates about $1.80 to $2.00 in total economic activity in the region.

Grower seats and grower regions would not change. New Mexico keeps its three Western grower seats, two for growers with 176 acres or more and one for smaller growers. USDA says the rule adds no industry cost beyond the late fees and interest.

Assessments are paid by handlers based on the weight of inshell pecans they handle. The penalties would hit only handlers who pay late. Whether any of that cost reaches growers through prices paid at the scale is not addressed in the proposal.

The proposal follows a separate vote by growers on whether to keep the marketing order at all. USDA held that continuance referendum July 6 through Aug. 3, 2026; the order requires one every five years.

Comments are due Dec. 9, 2026. Cite Docket AMS-SC-25-0881 and the Nov. 9, 2026, Federal Register, page 70809.

Comments are posted publicly without change. Background on the state's industry is on NMSU's pecan page.

item.title: In Memory of Samuel Firmin Aragon
item.description:
Samuel Firmin Aragon, age 69, of Alamogordo, passed away peacefully on October 30, 2026, surrounded by loved ones, after a hard-fought battle with cancer. Born to Patricio and Gavina Aragon on September 14, 1957, in Bernalillo, New Mexico. Samuel lived a life of curiosity, hard work, and an unwavering love for his family. Samuel also served his country with the National Guard and was later active with the U.S. Army from 1978 to 1979. item.title: In Memory of Faye Ragan
item.description:
Faye Ragan, a beloved wife, mother, and best friend, passed away on October 31, 2026, at home with her family. She was 78 years old. Born in northern Minnesota, her family relocated to Wisconsin where she graduated from Oak Creek High School. Following graduation, she enlisted in the Army where she met and married the love of her life and started a family in Wisconsin, before eventually retiring and relocating to Alamogordo. After a life filled with love, kindness, and laughter, Faye has now “retired from living” and been received by her Savior.

A creative soul and talented crafter, Faye loved making handmade gifts for others and was always ready to help those around her. She had a wonderful sense of humor, a love of animals (especially her fur-baby, Dallas), and a quirky obsession with making patterns in the carpet with her vacuum cleaner. A devoted child of God, a proud Army veteran, a popcorn connoisseur, an unsuccessful (yet persistent) gardener, and a loyal Minnesota Vikings fan, Faye brought her own unmistakable charm to the things she loved.

Faye is preceded in death by her parents Eugene and Lucille Turner and siblings Hal, David, Karen (Blake), and Jimmy Turner.

Faye is survived by her loving husband of 59 years, Johnny Ragan, her daughter, Michelle Ragan, and a host of other loving relatives and friends.

Though she will be deeply missed, the memories Faye created will live on in the hearts of all who knew and loved her.

The family extends our heartfelt gratitude to Faye’s caretaker, Victoria, and everyone at Ambercare Hospice for the comfort, compassion, and dignity they showed Faye and her family.

A private service and interment at Fort Stanton State Veterans Cemetery will be held at a later date.

item.title: Three Otero County Tracts Nominated for Opportunity Zone Status
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — All three census tracts Otero County put forward for federal Opportunity Zone status have been nominated by the state, county officials announced Monday.

The tracts cover Alamogordo's U.S. 54 Bypass corridor, the city's downtown and the Village of Tularosa. The New Mexico Economic Development Department released the governor's nominations on Nov. 2. The list now goes to the U.S. Treasury Department for designation covering 2027 through 2036.

If Treasury signs off, investors who put capital gains into housing, mixed-use and commercial projects in the three areas could qualify for federal tax breaks. A fourth Otero County tract, inside the Mescalero Apache Reservation, was also nominated.

The largest of the three, Census Tract 5.02, follows the Charlie T. Lee Memorial Relief Route and U.S. Highways 54, 70 and 82 along Alamogordo's western and northern edge. It already holds two major housing projects.

Sendero Alamo, an 88-unit apartment complex at 1200 Acacia Ave., is under construction. The county describes it as Alamogordo's first new multifamily project in 25 years. Envision Development & Construction has proposed Sacramento Springs, a 248-unit, three-phase community at 1450 Hamilton Road, backed by about $45 million in conventional financing.

The city is also weighing a Bypass Metropolitan Redevelopment Area covering 205 parcels in the corridor. The plan is due for a second hearing before the City Commission, and officials expect a final vote by year's end.

The other two tracts already have redevelopment plans in place:

Downtown Alamogordo (Tract 1) falls under the city's 2019 Downtown MRA. Work there includes the New York Avenue streetscape, rehabilitation of Dudley School and a Sacramento Mountains Foundation effort, with the Lakota Group, targeting 416 abandoned, vacant or deteriorated properties.

Tularosa (Tract 7.02) has had its own downtown MRA plan since 2015. Projects identified there include reactivating the Red Brick Building, the Granado Street historic district and new infill housing. Tularosa Gate Road in the tract is a main route into White Sands Missile Range.

Opportunity Zones were created by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act and renewed by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025. Investors can roll capital gains into projects in a designated zone. The tax on the original gain is deferred and reduced, and gains on the new investment are tax-free if it is held 10 years.

The county says its tracts qualify under the law's enhanced rural provisions. Those include a 30% basis step-up after five years and a lower, 50% threshold for the "substantial improvement" required of existing buildings. The county says the designation costs it and its municipalities nothing, since the benefit comes from federal tax savings. In a Facebook post Tuesday headed "Three for three," the county said it and its partners "put in nothing but the work," with the capital coming from outside investors.

New Mexico nominated 65 tracts statewide. The county's submission went through the Southeastern New Mexico Economic Development District, which also serves Lincoln, Chaves, Eddy and Lea counties.

The state's list also includes Census Tract 9400, which lies within the Mescalero Apache Reservation. The county congratulated the tribe and said use of any designation is up to the tribe, adding that it is ready to coordinate if asked.

"This is a decade of federal cost-of-capital leverage for Otero County," said Vickie Marquardt, chair of the Board of County Commissioners. She said residents, employers and families at Holloman Air Force Base stand to benefit.

County Manager Pamela Heltner said staff have a parcel inventory ready and are coordinating with Alamogordo and Tularosa to help developers through permitting and infrastructure planning.

County Attorney R.B. Nichols noted the county submitted three tracts in May and all three were nominated. "That does not happen by accident," he said, crediting the redevelopment plans paired with each tract. Nichols said the focus now shifts to attracting Qualified Opportunity Fund investors.

Adam Hoppes, executive director of the Alamogordo Chamber of Commerce, said the nominations give local businesses a tool to recruit investment and that members are ready to work with opportunity funds.

The nominations still require final approval from the Treasury Department. Questions about the downtown Alamogordo and Tularosa redevelopment areas go to those municipalities and their MainStreet programs. The Otero County Attorney's Office is handling questions about the Bypass corridor and countywide coordination, at (575) 437-7427.

Sources: Otero County Office of the County Attorney news release, Nov. 9, 2026; Otero County Administration Facebook post, Nov. 10, 2026.

item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Otero County Board of Commissioners meets at 9 a.m. today, Tuesday, Nov. 10, in Room 123 of the County Administration Building, 1101 New York Ave., with certification of the 2026 General Election results set for 10 a.m.

Commission Chairman Vickie Marquardt (District 3), Vice-Chairman Gerald Matherly (District 1) and Commissioner Amy Barela (District 2) face a 32-item agenda backed by a 756-page meeting packet.

Beyond routine business, the board is set to weigh in on four matters reaching well past county lines: the planned demolition of the Sacramento Peak Observatory at Sunspot, the proposed Union Pacific–Norfolk Southern railroad merger, a two-county economic development compact with Lincoln County, and who may hold stock water rights on public land.

Agenda packets list no county spending tied to any of those resolutions. The meeting's largest dollar figures instead come from state road and public safety funding and a jail health care contract, all on the consent agenda.

This morning , County Clerk Selina Maes will ask commissioners to certify the canvass of the 2026 General Election. Sitting as the county canvassing board, the commission's vote makes local results official one week after Election Day.

The agenda lists the canvass as a timed item, meaning it will be taken up at 10 a.m. even if other business is still underway.

The county is asking federal agencies to hold off on tearing down the Sacramento Peak Observatory campus until someone decides whether any of it should be saved.

The National Science Foundation announced Oct. 19 that it would demolish the Sunspot campus in two phases beginning in fiscal year 2027, with the first contract to be awarded by March 2027. Work already underway on the Dunn Solar Telescope is excluded. The campus covers about 76 buildings and structures on Lincoln National Forest land, including housing, a dormitory, a community center and a visitor center that drew 12,000 to 15,000 people a year.

The campus water and wastewater system also serves the neighboring Apache Point Observatory and the Otero County Fire District station at Sunspot. The county says it has not received the information it needs to judge how demolition would affect either one.

Resolution 115-28, presented by County Attorney RB Nichols, rests on two earlier federal documents. NSF's 2019 Record of Decision and a 2018 Programmatic Agreement say that if the Forest Service identifies a need to keep buildings or utilities, for itself or others, NSF would transfer them rather than demolish them. According to the packet, that evaluation has not been made.

The resolution would:

The resolution states it does not commit the county to acquire, run, fund or maintain anything at Sunspot. Any such decision would come back to the board.

Union Pacific asked the county for a letter supporting its proposed takeover of Norfolk Southern, which would create a single coast-to-coast railroad. Resolution 115-25 would give that support, with three local conditions attached.

The local stake is the Otero Siding Extension. Union Pacific plans to lengthen an existing siding about seven miles north of Tularosa to roughly 15,000 feet, so trains can meet and pass at up to 40 mph. The railroad estimates the cost at $11 million. The project was presented to Marquardt on Nov. 2.

Union Pacific's Carrizozo Subdivision runs through Alamogordo and Tularosa as a freight link between El Paso and the national network. The railroad says the merger would shift more than 2.1 million truckloads a year off highways. The county's draft letter notes that U.S. 54 and U.S. 70 carry heavy truck traffic through local communities.

Longer trains holding on a siding can block road crossings, however. The county wants the federal Surface Transportation Board to require:

The merger faces opposition from rival railroads BNSF, CSX and CPKC, shipper groups, rail unions and seven state attorneys general, mostly over national competition. The county's resolution says it takes no position on those issues. Under federal law the county cannot regulate the siding directly, Nichols wrote, so asking for conditions is its main way to protect local interests.

Comments are due to the Surface Transportation Board on Nov. 18. The resolution would authorize Marquardt to sign and Nichols to file them.

Resolution 115-27 would approve a memorandum of agreement creating the Otero–Lincoln Regional Economic Development Initiative, a joint marketing compact meant to pitch the two counties to employers as one market.

The board endorsed the concept in March. Otero County's population is about 70,400 and Lincoln County's about 19,800, a combined 90,200. That is nearly double the 50,000-person mark national site selectors use to screen markets, according to the packet. The model is the Clovis/Portales "Microplex," which the packet credits with drawing national retailers and a $200 million processing plant.

Sending the draft to Lincoln County was delayed through spring litigation and the Lincoln County fire emergency. Since then, Census Bureau commuting data has shown more than 1,000 workers crossing the county line daily. Nichols writes that the data meets the federal threshold for a Combined Statistical Area designation in four of the last five years.

Key terms of the agreement:

All eight incorporated municipalities in the two counties would be invited to join, starting with Alamogordo, which asked to be a full party. Holloman Air Force Base, NMSU-Alamogordo, ENMU-Ruidoso and smaller chambers are named as advisory invitees. The Mescalero Apache Tribe could join later.

The agreement takes effect only if the Lincoln County Commission also approves it. The resolution leaves blank which Otero commissioner will hold the county's steering committee seat. The packet lists no county spending tied to this action.

Three resolutions put the county on record ahead of next year's state and federal debates over land and water.

Stock water rights. Resolution 115-26 backs a draft bill for the 2027 legislative session on stock tanks built on state and federal land. Applicants for a stock water impoundment permit would have to show they own or control the livestock, are legally allowed to graze the land and have permission to build there. The draft also says owning or managing land does not, by itself, create a stock water right.

Nichols writes that the change would confirm that stock water belongs to the ranchers who build and use it, not to a land agency. He cites a 1978 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that national forests hold no reserved water rights for stock watering. His memo also flags likely opposition. The State Engineer called a similar 2025 bill unnecessary, and the State Land Office, federal agencies or conservation groups may object. The draft has no sponsor yet.

LANDS Act. Marquardt's Resolution 115-19 supports H.R. 10669, the Legislative Approval for National Designations Act. item.title: RPNM's Frozen SCC List: Who Gets to Vote, Who Holds Multiple Seats, and Is the Quorum Really 366?
item.description:
An opinion by Gary Person on election law, party rules, and transparency ahead of the January 9, 2027 state officer elections.

The Republican Party of New Mexico has announced that its State Central Committee (SCC) membership list was frozen November 4, 2026, and that 366 members are required for quorum at the January 9, 2027 state officer elections.

But after reviewing the 2026 election results, the SCC roster, and RPNM's own Uniform State Rules, a serious question emerges: How can the party confidently declare a fixed quorum when the eligibility of several members may change before the meeting?

There are four defeated Republican legislators, multiple individuals listed under more than one SCC position, and unresolved questions about when public officeholders legally cease to qualify for ex officio membership.

These issues deserve answers before ballots are distributed.

Four Defeated Legislators — Four Questions About Voting Rights

The November 3 election resulted in the defeat of four incumbent Republican state representatives:

All four appear on RPNM's September 30 SCC membership roster as ex officio members, based on their service in the New Mexico House of Representatives.

Under RPNM Uniform State Rule 2-1-3(A)(8)(f), incumbent Republican members of the New Mexico House qualify for SCC membership.

But what happens when they are no longer incumbent legislators?

That is where New Mexico law becomes particularly important.

What Does "Duly Qualified" Actually Mean?

The New Mexico Constitution establishes three important requirements.

Article XX, Section 1 requires elected officers to take and subscribe an oath before performing official duties.

Article XX, Section 2 provides that an officer remains in office until a successor has duly qualified.

Article XX, Section 3(A) establishes January 1 as the beginning of regular terms following the election.

Certification of election results, receiving a certificate of election, and becoming duly qualified are not necessarily the same legal event.

The 2026 election is scheduled for certification in November, with certificates of election scheduled for December 4. Yet the incoming legislative term does not begin until January 1.

So here is the question RPNM needs to answer:

If the four incoming Democratic representatives take their required oaths on December 31 and are otherwise qualified to assume office January 1, does that end the outgoing Republicans' ex officio membership before January 9?

Or, if those incoming representatives do not take their oaths until the Legislature convenes January 19, could the defeated Republicans remain in office under the constitutional holdover provision and retain SCC voting eligibility on January 9?

January 19 is the scheduled opening of the legislative session, not necessarily the date every incoming representative must qualify.

The precise dates of qualification must be established through official records.

RPNM should not assume that certification alone ends an incumbent's service, nor should it assume that the opening of the legislative session automatically determines when a successor becomes qualified.

How Can RPNM Freeze the SCC List on November 4?

The Official Call states:

"SCC LIST CLOSED 11/4/26 Quorum = 366"

Rule 1-3-1(B)(i) prohibits modification of the SCC membership list after an official meeting call is issued until that meeting concludes.

But Rule 2-1-3(A)(8)(f) ties legislative ex officio membership to being an incumbent Republican legislator.

This creates an obvious question about how RPNM intends to reconcile two rules.

If the four defeated Republicans cease to hold office before January 9, will RPNM still permit them to vote because their names were on the November 4 frozen list?

If their legislative qualifications expire, will the SCC remove their votes from the eligible membership calculation?

And if new Republican legislators assume office January 1, will those newly qualified ex officio members be excluded merely because their names were not on the November 4 list?

For example, Republican Heather Scott Ellison won House District 4 in November. Her incoming legislative status raises the opposite side of the same question.

The September roster also lists Andrea Reeb as an incumbent representative, although she resigned her legislative position in October. Was that change properly reflected before the November 4 freeze?

A frozen administrative roster and an individual's continuing legal eligibility are not necessarily identical. RPNM must explain which interpretation it is applying.

Why Are Some Individuals Listed Multiple Times?

The SCC roster raises another question about the distinction between holding multiple positions and having multiple SCC memberships.

RPNM Rule 2-1-3(B) provides for SCC membership through only one qualifying method, while Rule 2-1-3(D) allows each SCC member one vote.

The September 30 roster identifies:

NamePositions appearing on the SCC rosterRachel MartinezRPNM Second Vice-Chair, State Finance Committee Chair, Bernalillo County SCC Member #64Shona NeffRPNM Congressional District 2 Vice-Chair, Doña Ana County SCC Member #16James TownsendRepublican National Committeeman, New Mexico Senator District 34Rosalind TrippFormer Republican National Committeewoman, Socorro County Treasurer

The roster marks one entry for each individual with a Q value of 1 and the additional entries with 0.

That suggests RPNM is attempting to prevent duplicate counting.

But preventing multiple votes does not fully answer whether someone should continue occupying more than one SCC position.

If an individual already qualifies through an ex officio position, what happens to an elected county SCC position also listed under that individual's name?

Can someone else represent that county through the elected position?

Or can the same person continue occupying the additional position indefinitely, even if it does not provide another vote?

These are distinct questions that deserve answers.

Rachel Martinez: Three Positions, One Vote — But What About Representation?

Rachel Martinez presents the clearest example.

She appears three times in the September SCC roster:

RPNM's position that she receives only one vote is consistent with the one-vote rule and the roster's Q markings.

But the more important question concerns representation.

Why does Rachel Martinez remain listed in three SCC positions when the Uniform State Rules provide for membership through only one qualifying method?

If the Bernalillo County position is not being counted as her voting membership, is that position still considered occupied?

Has another qualified Republican requested the opportunity to serve in that position?

Has Martinez declined to relinquish it, and if so, what rule permits the position to remain under her name?

Those questions require documentary answers. The roster itself does not establish that she refused a request to step aside or that a replacement was improperly denied.

Nevertheless, if an elected county SCC position is being held under a non-counting entry, RPNM should explain whether that position is available to another qualified Republican and, if not, why not.

The same principle warrants examination for Shona Neff and Rosalind Tripp, who also have county positions marked Q = 0.

James Townsend's two ex officio qualifications raise the related question of how the party records and counts overlapping sources of membership.

One vote per person is clear. What constitutes one legally occupied SCC position deserves equal clarity.

The Real Problem: Is 366 an Accurate Quorum?

Rule 2-1-5(C) requires two-thirds of SCC members representing two-thirds of New Mexico's 33 counties to establish quorum.

That means the SCC must satisfy both the numerical requirement and representation from at least 22 counties.

Yet RPNM declared a quorum of 366 when the Official Call was issued November 4.

Since then, the scheduled transition of elected public offices presents several unresolved eligibility questions.

The four defeated Republican representatives may cease qualifying as ex officio SCC members before January 9.Newly elected Republican legislators may become qualified. Additional SCC positions remain listed under individuals already counted through another method.

There is also the question of how 2026 gubernatorial election results affect future county SCC apportionment under Rule 2-1-3(A)(2), which bases elected representation on the last preceding gubernatorial election for which official canvass records are available.

That apportionment issue must be reconciled with the November 4 roster freeze rather than assumed to change the January 9 roster automatically.

The result is a disputed membership calculation.

A frozen roster may establish the list RPNM intends to use, but it does not, without further explanation, settle every question about legal eligibility, overlapping membership qualifications, or who may actually vote.

The quorum figure may remain administratively fixed under RPNM's interpretation of its rules. However, whether that figure accurately reflects qualified membership on January 9 remains unresolved.

Until RPNM explains these matters, the effective quorum is a moving target in dispute, even if the official announcement continues to say 366.

Where Is the Advisory State Rules Committee?

This is exactly the kind of rules-conformity issue that deserves a clear response from state party leadership.

Mark VanDyke, chairman of the Advisory State Rules Committee, should be asked for the committee's interpretation of the apparent conflict between the frozen SCC list and changing ex officio qualifications.

Mike Nelson, serving as acting state chairman, and Kathleen Apodaca, state secretary, should be asked to provide the approved roster, credentials procedures, and quorum calculation.

The Advisory State Rules Committee has defined duties under Rule 2-1-8(B), including reviewing the Uniform State Rules for conformity with law. That does not make it the final adjudicator of every election dispute, but its written analysis would help clarify the party's position.

The SCC itself remains the party's governing body.

The Questions Every SCC Member Deserves Answered

Before January 9, RPNM leadership should publicly explain:

None of these questions should be dismissed simply because the party already published an official call.

Transparency Should Come Before the Vote

New Mexico Republicans have already watched their party suffer significant election losses in 2026.

Now they face a state officer election in which the membership list is frozen, multiple people appear under more than one qualifying position, and four defeated legislators may or may not remain eligible to vote depending on when their successors become duly qualified.

RPNM has every opportunity to provide the records, explain the rules, and resolve these uncertainties before the election.

The SCC cannot confidently determine whether it has a lawful quorum without first determining who is legally entitled to be counted.

A published number is not a substitute for a transparent calculation.

Before RPNM elects its next leadership, it needs to answer a much simpler question: Who actually belongs to the State Central Committee on January 9, 2027, and how can the party prove it?

The credibility of the election depends on those answers.

Primary references: RPNM Uniform State Rules effective September 6, 2025, particularly Rules 1-3-1(B)(i), 2-1-3(A)–(D), 2-1-5(C) and 2-1-8(B); Q3 SCC Membership List dated September 30, 2026; November 4, 2026 Official Call; New Mexico Constitution, Article XX, Sections 1–3; New Mexico Secretary of State election and oath-of-office guidance.

item.title: In Memory of Rita Anne Lackey
item.description:
Rita Anne Lackey, 79, of Alamogordo, New Mexico, passed away peacefully at home on November 3, 2026, surrounded by her family.

Rita was born on August 23, 1947, in Allegany, New York, to Geddes and Betty Kujaneck. She graduated from Alamogordo High School in 1965 and married Norman later that year. After she graduated from Baptist Bible College in Springfield, Missouri, the couple answered a call to serve the Lord as missionaries in Ethiopia, East Africa, where they remained until 1977. They later continued their missionary work in Puerto Rico from 1979 to 1983.

Rita was a longtime member of La Luz Bible Church, where she taught Sunday School and her church family was a cherished part of her life. She knew how much the Lord had done for her, and she loved sharing the joy of knowing Him with others.

Art was a lifelong passion for Rita. She painted and drew, and she taught art classes to many students. She also loved music and spending time outdoors.

Rita dearly loved her family. She is survived by her husband of 61 years, Norman Lackey; her children, Carissa (Pete) Pittman, Nathan Lackey, Jennifer (Alex) Burks, and Rachel (Justin) Burks; nine grandchildren; two great-grandchildren; and her brother, Dan Kujaneck.

She was preceded in death by her parents, Geddes and Betty Kujaneck; her brother, Bryan Kujaneck; and her daughter-in-law, Cynthia Lujan Lackey.

A memorial service will be held on Saturday, December 5, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. at La Luz Bible Church in La Luz, New Mexico.

item.title: Lawmakers' paycheck arrives without ethics rules; think tank maps the missing guardrails
item.description:
SANTA FE — New Mexico legislators will start drawing salaries in 2029, but the measure voters approved Nov. 3 adds no ethics rules to go with the money. A new report from Think New Mexico lays out the guardrails that are missing.

The Santa Fe think tank's new report lays out four groups of reforms: mandatory disclosure and recusal on conflicts of interest, a two-year wait before former lawmakers can lobby, broader lobbyist disclosure, and new rules on dark money and fake constituent messages.

Constitutional Amendment 4 passed roughly 62% to 38% in preliminary returns. It ties pay to the state's median household income, about $68,000, ending New Mexico's status as the last state with an unsalaried legislature. The amendment sets pay only; it contains no new rules on conflicts of interest, outside income or lobbying.

That gap is the concern Alamogordo Town News raised before the election. Its editorial board urged a no vote on Oct. 27, arguing the amendment wrote a paycheck without defining the job or the ethics standards that should come with it.

Think New Mexico's report reaches a similar conclusion: states that pay legislators generally hold them to stricter rules, and New Mexico's volunteer status has long been the excuse for loose ones.

It also points to recent scandals. On Aug. 14, former House Majority Leader Sheryl Williams Stapleton was convicted of 31 federal felonies, including bribery and money laundering, for diverting more than $2 million in education funds meant for Albuquerque students. A 2025 Garrity Group survey found only 19% of New Mexicans trust state government officials, down from 31% in 2020.

A BSP Research poll commissioned by the group, conducted July 22 to Aug. 10, found 64% of voters back paying legislators only if mandatory ethics reforms come with it.

Alamogordo Town News editor Chris Edwards laid out the case against Amendment 4 in an Oct. 27 commentary. The amendment, he wrote, sets a salary for 112 legislators without defining the work it pays for.

Nothing in the measure requires minimum hours, town halls, district offices, constituent-service standards or attendance at interim committees. It places no limit on outside income, so a member could collect the full salary while keeping a full-time career.

The commentary also put a price on the job:

About $65 an hour. Supporters cite a self-reported average of 20 hours a week. At roughly $67,800 a year, that works out to about $65 an hour.

Nearly $90,000 a year. Legislators keep their $247-a-day per diem, mileage and pension. In a 60-day session year, salary plus session per diem reaches $82,620, and passes $87,500 with 20 interim committee days.

Room for more. The amendment deletes the constitutional ban on other "perquisites or allowances," letting a future Legislature add benefits for itself.

The editorial board called for a new amendment next session that defines the job, addresses outside employment and conflicts of interest, and lets an independent citizens commission set pay.

Think New Mexico's package answers the conflict-of-interest piece of that critique. It does not address minimum duties or who sets legislative pay, which Town News flagged as equally urgent.

The centerpiece is a constitutional amendment requiring salaried legislators to recuse themselves from bills in which they have a direct financial stake, without needing their colleagues' permission.

Under current House and Senate rules, a lawmaker cannot simply recuse. The chamber must vote to excuse them. The report counts New Mexico among just nine states where recusal is discouraged, while 36 states expect it. Colorado, Oklahoma and Texas write the requirement into their constitutions.

The group wants a constitutional change rather than a statute because a February 2026 State Ethics Commission advisory opinion said each chamber controls its own members' voting, leaving a law open to challenge.

The test would be whether a bill helps or hurts a legislator more than the public at large. A teacher-legislator could vote on the overall education budget but not on a bill raising retired teachers' pensions.

The report also calls for:

Requiring legislators to disclose financial conflicts before acting on a bill, as 43 states do, following Colorado's model.

Requiring disclosure when a spouse, parent, child or sibling is paid to lobby on a bill, as the Ethics Commission has recommended, and recusal when the lobbyist is a spouse.

Rewriting the Financial Disclosure Act so officials name the specific businesses and assets behind income over $5,000, instead of broad categories like "investment income," and report honoraria and debts. Dollar amounts would stay private.

Polling found 81% support for recusal on direct conflicts and 78% for disclosing family members' lobbying.

The second proposal would bar former legislators from lobbying for pay for two years after leaving office. Today, a lawmaker could legally resign mid-session and be paid to lobby former colleagues the next day.

Thirty-seven states have such waiting periods, most of one or two years. Florida's is six. Members of Congress have been covered since 1989, and New Mexico executive branch employees have faced a one-year ban since 1993. The report would lengthen that executive branch ban to two years for consistency.

The idea has drawn bipartisan support before. A 2017 two-year ban passed the House 58-2 but died in the Senate Judiciary Committee, and Sen. Harold Pope has introduced versions in 2023, 2025 and 2026. Former Govs. Bill Richardson, a Democrat, and Susana Martinez, a Republican, both backed it.

The ban would not stop former lawmakers from advocating unpaid. Sixty-six percent of voters supported it; 10% opposed.

Registered lobbyists outnumber New Mexico legislators about six to one, and their reported spending hit a record $1.25 million by October 2025. Yet the Center for Public Integrity gave the state an F for lobbying disclosure, ranking it 43rd.

The report cites filings that reveal little. One lobbyist with 19 clients reported $22,710 spent on flowers for legislators. Another listed 31 restaurant meals for "various legislators and staff" without naming clients or bills.

Think New Mexico proposes four changes to the Lobbyist Regulation Act:

The report estimates lobbyists received more than $7.8 million in unreported pay in 2025, based on national ratios of compensation to spending.

The bill-tracking idea came close in 2025. House Bill 143, sponsored by Rep. Sarah Silva and Sen. Jeff Steinborn, passed both chambers but was vetoed by the governor. Colorado requires lobbyists to disclose a bill position within 72 hours.

State law requires groups that buy political ads to disclose their donors, but only their direct donors. The report shows how that leaves voters guessing.

New Chapter New Mexico PAC spent $438,198 in the 2026 primary; its only contributor was a nonprofit of the same name, which need not reveal its funders. Accountable New Mexico got 88.7% of its $975,500 from one nonprofit. Elevate New Mexico, which ran ads for the Project Jupiter data center, drew all of its $3.67 million from a single LLC.

The group proposes a "true source" law modeled on Arizona's Voters' Right to Know Act, approved by 72% of Arizona voters in 2022 and upheld by that state's Supreme Court in June. Big spenders would name donors over $5,000, and those donors would name their own funders until the original source is reached. Ads would list their top three donors and the share of out-of-state money. It would cover both campaign and issue ads.

The report also recommends:

Seventy-one percent of voters supported requiring ad sponsors to report their funding sources.

Most of the proposals could be passed as ordinary bills in the 60-day legislative session that opens in January. The recusal requirement would need lawmakers to put another constitutional amendment before voters.

Many of the ideas have stalled before, often in Senate committees. The report argues that the new salaries change the calculus, and that the State Ethics Commission already endorses several of the reforms. The group frames the package as bringing New Mexico in line with what most states already require.

Think New Mexico, a nonpartisan think tank founded in 1999, says it accepts no government funding. The report notes that it was researched and written without artificial intelligence.

item.title: Commentary: Otero County's lawmakers, their ethics votes, and the guardrails New Mexico still needs.
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Before New Mexico voters approved paying legislators a salary, the Legislature took recorded votes on two lobbyist-transparency bills and on the pay amendment itself. Every Otero County legislator voted no on every one of those measures that came before them.

The votes matter as lawmakers prepare for a January session in which Think New Mexico is pressing a package of ethics reforms: recusal on conflicts of interest, a two-year lobbying ban for ex-legislators, fuller lobbyist disclosure and limits on dark money. (Read our story on those proposals.)

Otero County is represented by Rep. John Block (R-Alamogordo, House District 51), Rep. Jonathan Henry (R, House District 54), Sen. Jim Townsend (R, Senate District 34) and Sen. Rex Wilson (R, Senate District 33). Wilson was appointed in January 2026, replacing Sen. Nicholas Paul of Alamogordo, who resigned for health reasons. Rep. Sarah Silva (D-Las Cruces, House District 53), a neighboring southern New Mexico lawmaker, sponsored both lobbying bills.

House Bill 143 (2025) would have required lobbyists to file a report within 48 hours of lobbying on a bill, naming the bill, the client and the position taken. It is the bill-tracking reform Think New Mexico now recommends.

Republicans argued the bill did not go far enough. A House Republican amendment to limit lobbyist spending on lawmakers' meals and drinks was stripped in the Senate. They offered amendments requiring lobbyists to disclose gifts to lawmakers, including food and drink, and requiring grassroots groups to disclose lobbying. Democrats defeated both.

House Bill 164 (2026), a revised version from Silva and Sen. Jeff Steinborn, died on a 32-32 tie on Feb. 14, 2026. Block and Henry again voted no. The vote did not split on party lines: several Democrats, including Reps. Patricia Lundstrom and Linda Serrato, voted no, and Republican Rep. Nicole Chavez voted yes.

The bill died by the narrowest possible margin. A single no vote switched to yes, including from either Otero County House member, would have broken the tie.

House Joint Resolution 5 (2026) put Constitutional Amendment 4 on the ballot, setting legislator pay at the state median household income starting in 2029. It carried no minimum duties, outside-income limits or new ethics rules.

Republicans did try to attach guardrails. In the House, Henry offered an amendment barring per diem on top of a salary for work close to home; Democrats voted it down. In the Senate, Democrats rejected Republican amendments for 16-year term limits and for ending per diem for meetings within 50 miles of a legislator's home.

A competing approach from Republican Sens. Craig Brandt and Pat Boone, Senate Joint Resolution 2, would have had an independent citizens commission set legislative pay, paired with term limits. It did not reach the ballot. That is the model Town News's editorial board urged before the election.

The local delegation's no votes on HJR 5 line up with Town News's objection to pay without guardrails. But their no votes on the lobbying bills cut the other way: those bills were among the few transparency measures to reach a floor vote.

Voters approved a salary. They did not approve a blank check. Three guardrails proposed in the 2025 and 2026 sessions deserve a second chance now that lawmakers will be paid.

Legislators collect $247 a day in per diem during sessions and interim meetings, on top of mileage and a pension. Starting in 2029 they will also draw about $67,800 a year. In a 60-day session year, salary plus session per diem alone reaches $82,620, according to Town News's October analysis.

Per diem exists to cover the cost of being away from home. Paying it to a lawmaker who sleeps in their own bed after a meeting across town is extra pay, not reimbursement. The legislator pension is also calculated from the per diem rate, so every per diem increase raises retirement pay too.

The fixes are modest. Henry's House amendment would have barred per diem on top of salary for work close to home. Senate Republicans proposed ending per diem for meetings within 50 miles of a legislator's home. SJR 2 would have tied per diem to the federal government's lodging rate for Santa Fe. Democrats rejected the first two; SJR 2 never got a hearing.

Lobbyist spending on New Mexico lawmakers set a record in 2025, passing $1.25 million by October. Current reports rarely say which legislators were treated. One 2026 filing listed $22,710 on flowers for legislators; another listed 31 restaurant meals for "various legislators and staff."

State law caps gifts from lobbyists at $250 per donor per year, but meals and entertainment still flow freely during session. In 2025 the House adopted a Republican amendment to HB 143 that many read as a $50-a-day cap on lobbyist spending per legislator during session. The Senate Rules Committee stripped it out.

The bill's Senate sponsor, Sen. Jeff Steinborn, called the cap a distraction from disclosure but said he would back a full ban on such meals in separate legislation. That opening should be taken. A paid legislator has less reason to accept a free dinner from someone seeking their vote.

Sixteen states limit how long legislators may serve. New Mexico does not. In 2026, Senate Republicans proposed a 16-year cap as an amendment to HJR 5, and Sens. Craig Brandt and Pat Boone proposed a 12-year cap in SJR 2. The amendment was rejected and SJR 2 was postponed indefinitely on its first day.

The case is strongest now. A salary turns a citizen post into a paying job, and limits keep it from becoming a career. Turnover breaks up long-standing relationships between lawmakers and the lobbyists who court them, and it opens seats to newcomers in a district like Henry's, where he ran unopposed this year.

Term limits carry real costs, covered below. A 12- to 16-year cap is long enough to let lawmakers build expertise while still forcing regular renewal.

The per diem, meal-cap and term-limit amendments were decided without a recorded roll call, so no individual votes exist in the Legislature's or LegiScan's records. SJR 2 died before any vote. The Legislature broadcasts floor sessions, and these lawmakers can be asked directly where they stand.

Most of what Think New Mexico now proposes has never reached a floor vote, so there is no recorded position for local lawmakers.

The State Ethics Commission cannot carry this load alone, and its own rules show why.

Real accountability means rules with consequences voters can see:

These ideas have serious opponents, and readers should weigh their arguments.

The 60-day legislative session opens Tuesday, Jan. 19, 2027. Block, Henry and Silva won re-election Nov. 3, Wilson won his seat outright, and Townsend's term runs through 2028. All five will be voting. Gov.-elect Deb Haaland takes office Jan. 1, 2027, and will decide whether any reform that passes becomes law.

Lawmakers voted themselves a path to a paycheck. Now it is your turn to set the terms. Call or email every official below before the session opens. Ask each one, by name, to commit publicly to:

Your Otero County legislators

Neighboring southern New Mexico lawmaker

Legislative leadership, which decides which bills get heard

State party leadership

The incoming governor's office

Not sure who represents you? Use the Legislature's district finder.

Capitol offices are staffed mainly during session; email works year-round. A reform that dies in committee never reaches your legislator's vote, so contact leadership, both parties and the governor's office too. Ask for a yes or no. Write down the answer. Then hold them to it at the ballot box.

Related coverage

Official records, HB 143 (2025)

Official records, HB 164 (2026)

Official records, HJR 5 (2026)

Legislators

Guardrails and enforcement

Make the call. Send the email. Demand term limits, a job description and real accountability before the session opens Jan. 19.

item.title: Alamogordo Christmas Miracle Returns for Fifth Year, Calls for Gifts for Babies and Teens
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Alamogordo Christmas Miracle is back for its fifth year, and organizer Daniel Acuña has a simple request for holiday shoppers: don't forget the babies and the teenagers.

Speaking with Anthony Lucero on KALH Radio, Acuña said the annual toy drive and community giveaway will take place Saturday, Dec. 12, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at Desert Suds Car Wash, which has partnered with the group to host the event.

"Last year we had 400 families come out," Acuña said, "and we helped out a bunch of kids."

The drive collects toys for children from birth through age 17. Acuña said donations tend to cluster around kids roughly 6 to 11, leaving the youngest and oldest children short.

For teenagers, he suggested electronics, sports gear such as footballs, basketballs and soccer balls, personal-care items like deodorant and body wash, and cosmetics, compact mirrors and nail kits.

Collection boxes are set up around town, including two at the Ford dealership, Albertsons, the Classic Desert Aire Hotel, Drinkwell on New York Avenue, Rope Insurance, the Border Patrol, White Sands Dental, George Gandhi, and Jr's Auto Service. New boxes are expected this week at Desert Paws, Betty Dare RE/MAX and Southwest Sound Healing.

Cash donations are also welcome for those unsure what to buy. Gonzalez Lawn, one of the event's platinum sponsors, recently gave $500 toward toys.

Families do not need to sign up in advance, but children must be present to receive a gift. Along with the toy giveaway, the day will feature a live DJ, a car show by Immaculate Car Club, food trucks, vendors, and raffles. Acuña also credited the Saturday market vendors who regularly support the event and will be on hand with crafts for last-minute shoppers.

To donate, volunteer or get more information, contact Acuña through the Alamogordo Christmas Miracle Facebook page, his personal Facebook page (Daniel Acuña), or by phone at 505-410-1375. He stressed that the area code is 505, not 575.

"If you know any kids that need presents this year, send them our way," Acuña said, "and we'll get them something good."

Watch the full interview on Krazy KALH Radio: https://youtu.be/yknacjPDvBw

item.title: Otero County asks feds to pause Sunspot demolition, certifies 2026 election
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — The Otero County Commission on Tuesday, Nov. 10, formally asked the National Science Foundation and the Lincoln National Forest to hold off on tearing down the historic Sacramento Peak Observatory campus at Sunspot. The county wants an independent assessment of which buildings can be saved before any more come down.

The resolution was the centerpiece of a long meeting. Commissioners also certified the 2026 general election canvass, backed a Union Pacific–Norfolk Southern railroad merger with conditions, and approved a regional economic development pact with Lincoln County. They passed a 17-item consent agenda carrying more than $10 million in state infrastructure money.

Chair Vickie Marquardt and Commissioners Gerald Matherly and Amy Barela were all present. The meeting opened with a Veterans Day proclamation honoring the roughly 40 veterans on the county payroll and World War II tank hero Willie E. Estrada, an Otero County native.

Resolution 11-10-26/115-28 asks the NSF and the Forest Service to defer demolition pending a public reuse evaluation. It also requests records on the campus water system and asks that the county be confirmed as a consulting party in the federal historic preservation review. It passed on a motion by Commissioner Matherly.

County Attorney R.B. Nichols said the NSF plans to demolish the campus in phases. A contract has already been awarded to take down the Richard B. Dunn Solar Telescope, where leaking mercury was found earlier this year. A contract for the remaining structures could be awarded anytime between now and March, he said.

Those later phases would take in housing, a dormitory, a community center and a visitor center that drew 12,000 to 15,000 people a year. They would also take in the community water and wastewater system that serves the neighboring Apache Point Observatory and the county's own Sunspot fire station.

Nichols pointed to the NSF's 2019 record of decision, which says buildings or utilities are to be transferred rather than demolished if the Forest Service or another entity identifies a need for them. A 2018 programmatic agreement contemplates the same outcome. "As far as I can tell, that evaluation has not been done," he said.

"Remediation is going to be required, whether the buildings are demolished or preserved," Nichols said. The question, he argued, is whether a building needs "$10,000" of work or is "a $10 million project to save a $500,000 building. We don't know because that detailed assessment has not occurred."

He acknowledged the county is "late to the game." It was not asked to the table, and the issue drew little attention until the mercury leak. But he said New Mexico State University has signaled it would continue research and run the visitor center if an operator can be found for the buildings. NMSU has also obtained quotes for two economic studies on astrotourism potential.

The county has sent the NSF two letters. Nichols said the agency acknowledged them Monday, referred them to its Freedom of Information Act office and classified the county as a "commercial requester." He has written back asking the agency to correct that and to answer the county's request for a pause.

Nichols also raised a federal notice requirement. He said the appropriations act Congress passed in January requires the NSF to notify House and Senate appropriators 30 days before divesting any facility worth more than $2.5 million. The NSF moved ahead with demolition a month after that law took effect and has since obligated at least $13.7 million, he said. He asked the county's congressional delegation to find out whether that notice was given.

Earlier in the meeting, acting Lincoln National Forest Supervisor Cecilia Clavette said the Forest Service shares the goal of preserving Sunspot's history but not its buildings. "We do not believe preserving that history requires preserving the unsafe or deteriorating buildings," she said.

She described an 80-year-old site with asbestos, lead paint and failing utilities, including asbestos water piping underground. Returning the buildings to public use "would require extensive remediation and substantial reinvestment," she said. The current plan grew out of a process that began in 2016 with environmental analysis, historic review and public comment.

Clavette said the agency wants to work with the county on the site's future after cleanup, including a dark-sky recreation area, and on the best path forward for the fire station. Nichols said the Forest Service's vision includes a campground and new visitor center, with most existing buildings removed. Agency officials told him rehabilitation is cost-prohibitive and not in their budget.

Matherly questioned whether demolition is really cheaper. Abatement of asbestos and lead must be paid for either way, he noted, so sealing up some buildings might cost less than tearing them down and hauling debris off the mountain. His top concern, he said, is keeping the water system that is "essential for the mountain community safety."

He also challenged the plan for the Dunn telescope, whose structure extends about 220 feet underground. He said he understood it would be cut down below grade and covered with dirt. That falls short of the full reclamation the Forest Service demands of others, he said, citing the county's old Tully motocross track. "I just want everybody to play by the same rules."

Marquardt said the issue "is just coming to a head now" after years in the works, accelerated by the mercury cleanup. After the vote she told supporters, "We're gonna keep fighting."

Dave Dooling, president of the Sunspot Community Center and the observatory's education officer from 2002 to 2012, said the Dunn's mercury has been removed. It is being held on site in a secure container while the NSF negotiates with the Department of Energy to store it, he said.

His understanding is that the telescope's pieces will be cut away and dropped into the 220-foot pit below, which will then be capped. "There's no contact with an aquifer," he said. He described the $13.7 million as covering assessment, mercury removal and the Dunn's demolition. Later phases could run $15 million to $25 million based on an old NSF estimate adjusted for inflation, he said.

Dooling named three buildings as most worth saving: the visitor center, the Evans Solar Facility and the Hilltop Dome. He said the latter two mainly suffer from peeling paint and could be "mothballed" — an option the NSF itself once considered — until grant money is found. Lead paint and asbestos must be removed before any bulldozing anyway, he noted, "otherwise you turn that stuff into dust" and spread it through the woods.

He said improvements could come in stages and that the community center "could start with dry camping tomorrow if the NSF will let us do it." Sunspot rates a 2 on the 9-point Bortle dark-sky scale, he said: "just about as good as it gets."

Asked whether the county could seek a cease-and-desist order, Dooling said lawyers have told supporters it is hard to direct the federal government on its own property. A cultural heritage lawyer, Ricardo St. Hilaire of New Hampshire, has filed records requests on their behalf, he said. He expects work on the Dunn to start around January, with its contract running through March 23.

Heidi Sanchez, who worked at Sunspot for eight years, spoke remotely after technical trouble. "I'm not saying every building must be saved," she said. "But age alone should not be the justification for demolition. In fact, age is often what makes a place worthy of preservation." She urged a coalition of partners rather than reliance on any single agency. "Once these structures come down, there is no second chance."

Claudia Powell, who spent 10 years with Alamogordo MainStreet, said the architect behind some of Sunspot's 1950s buildings also designed buildings at Los Alamos and the State Capitol Roundhouse. Apart from the science, she said, "this is a really valuable piece of property that we should work really hard to save."

Commissioners certified the canvass of the 2026 general election after a report from County Clerk Selena May. She said 18,158 ballots were cast, for 42% turnout. Same-day registration added 184 voters during early voting and 329 on Election Day.

All polling locations balanced, May said. One provisional ballot was accepted, and 189 ballots were hand-tallied: 80 regular and 109 from military and overseas voters. Ten absentee ballots were rejected — four for missing signatures or Social Security digits, and six with no outer envelope or with the identifying sticker removed.

The one significant problem came in Chaparral, where a polling site ran low on ballot paper. Replacement stock borrowed from Doña Ana County turned out to be 17-inch paper, not Otero's 14-inch, and 26 voters waited about 15 minutes for the right stock. "Longest 15 minutes of my life," May said. Everyone in line got to vote.

May said this was the last election in Room 101 of the county administration building. On Sheriff David Black's advice, the clerk's office will no longer hold early voting there because the building must stay open to the public for long stretches. Officials cited people entering to use the restrooms, including at least one homeless person this cycle. The county is seeking a new early voting site and has until next June to set polling locations.

The consent agenda passed in a single vote. Major items included:

VitalCore Health Strategies renewal, jail medical and mental health care

$2,446,919.97

Colonias infrastructure loan/grant, Bent–Round Mountain Road drainage and roadway

The board also endorsed New Mexico Counties' 2027 legislative priorities, November budget adjustments, an FY2027 sick leave buyback and quarterly financial reports. It awarded the state lobbyist contract to DeVore Aragon.

The commission closed with an executive session to discuss litigation and the purchase, acquisition or disposal of real property.

item.title: Diaz Runs to Fourth as Mescalero Apache, Cloudcroft Close Season at State

Stephie Prins (74th, 26:03.97) and Verbena Comanche (75th, 26:22.78) crossed the line just seconds apart to round out the scoring five, followed by Ellie Gallerito (82nd, 27:30.78) and Lariah Comanche (86th, 28:16.02).
