item.title: The Doctor Is In: Could the City Have Settled Its Open Meetings Fight for Less?
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Former City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez says the Alamogordo City Commission could have resolved its Open Meetings Act dispute months ago, without running up outside legal bills. She made the case on this week's "The Doctor Is In" segment with host Anthony Lucero on KALH Radio.

The segment centers on the citizen lawsuit over the hiring of City Manager Robert Stockwell. Chris Edwards and Concerned Citizens of Alamogordo filed the petition in the Twelfth Judicial District Court on June 2, 2026, after giving the City written notice of the alleged violations on May 5 (background). A judge has since refused to dismiss the case, and it is headed for a hearing on the merits (court ruling).

"Could this have been resolved months ago without spending taxpayer dollars on outside legal representation?" Hernandez asked.

Hernandez said that while she was still city manager, she recommended the Commission acknowledge a potential violation, disclose it voluntarily and take corrective action.

State law gives public bodies room to do that. Before a citizen can sue, the public body gets written notice and 15 days to act on the claim, and it can reconsider a challenged action at a properly noticed public meeting. Violations are also a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of up to $500 per offense against an individual who is convicted.

"To me, voluntarily identifying and correcting a potential violation seemed far less costly than prolonged litigation," she said. She added that a voluntary fix could still be an option today, though it would not guarantee the lawsuit is dismissed.

Hernandez also addressed concerns raised at the time that she had a conflict of interest, since the dispute involved hiring her successor. Her recommendation, she said, was about protecting the City and taxpayers, not about who should hold the job.

Hernandez pointed to Commissioner Baxter Pattillo's description of doing the legwork on Stockwell's proposed contract and circulating documents to the Commission.

That, she said, raises the possibility of a rolling quorum: commissioners discussing public business through a series of private communications that together involve a quorum. She was careful to note that circulating documents is not necessarily a violation on its own, but said it raises questions worth examining.

Hernandez acknowledged the law is complicated. She said she has worked with it for seven years and still doesn't consider herself an expert. Still, she noted, the Commission received Open Meetings Act training in March and has had earlier training opportunities.

Hernandez pushed back on the idea that the City can simply recover its legal bills from the citizen if it prevails.

Under the Open Meetings Act, a winning public body is awarded court costs. It recovers attorney fees only if the court also finds the plaintiff sued without sufficient information and belief that good grounds supported the case (NMSA 10-15-3).

"A citizen seeking government transparency doesn't automatically become responsible for the City's attorney fees simply because they lose a lawsuit," she said. The longer the case runs, she added, the higher the bills climb.

"Government officials make mistakes. What matters is how they respond," Hernandez said. "Shouldn't protecting taxpayer dollars be just as important as winning a lawsuit?"

Hear the full conversation with Dr. Stephanie Hernandez and Anthony Lucero on "The Doctor Is In": Open Meetings Act — The Doctor Is In (YouTube). More programming at KALHRadio.org.

Disclosure: Chris Edwards, general manager of KALH Radio and Alamogordo Town News, is the petitioner in the lawsuit discussed here. The case continues with an expected motion ruling within a week and a court conference to discuss next steps.

item.title: 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News Alamogordo Honors Its Veterans on Veterans Day 2026
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — At 11 a.m. today, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, Alamogordo pauses to honor the men and women who have worn the uniform of the United States. In a city whose story has been tied to Holloman Air Force Base since 1942, Veterans Day is not an abstraction. It is the neighbor down the street, the retiree at the VFW, and the Airman who just came home from deployment.

The 108th anniversary of the World War I armistice falls midweek this year, so the community began its tribute early. Since Saturday, residents have lined 10th Street, filled the civic center and gathered at the airport to say thank you.

The observances opened Saturday, Nov. 7, with the annual Veterans Day Parade down 10th Street from Cuba Avenue to Maryland Avenue. The free parade was organized by Air Force Sergeants Association Chapter 1257 at Holloman (Town News).

Airmen of the 49th Wing marched alongside cadets of the Alamogordo High School Air Force Junior ROTC, and the Tiger marching band played the route (DVIDS). The Patriot Guard Riders staged that morning at Mountain View Church on Cuba Avenue to ride in the procession (Patriot Guard Riders).

The same day, the Alamogordo-White Sands Regional Airport held a free Open House and Veterans Appreciation Day with aircraft displays, food trucks and STEM activities. The city's Sounds of Freedom celebration filled Alameda Park (City of Alamogordo). On Tuesday night, AFSA Chapter 1257 hosted its 13th annual Veterans Appreciation Dinner at the Sgt. Willie Estrada Memorial Civic Center, free to local veterans and a guest.

Few New Mexico communities are as bound to the armed forces as Alamogordo. This past May, the city and Holloman received the 2025 Altus Community Support Award, their second win in three years (Holloman AFB). The honor recognizes the city's backing of the base and its families.

That bond keeps growing. In June the 49th Wing welcomed Col. Michael S. Mullin as commander, back for a second tour, as the wing moved to Air Combat Command (Town News). In July six 49th Wing Airmen, including two Security Forces leaders awarded the Bronze Star, were recognized for combat service in the Middle East (Air University). They are today's veterans in the making.

The city's older generations are honored, too. In April, Vietnam-era veterans Chris Hall and Lucio Vazquez came home from a Rio Grande Honor Flight trip to Washington, D.C., to a hero's welcome at Patron's Hall (Town News). Over Memorial Day weekend, more than 70 volunteers joined VFW Post 7686 at dawn to place flags on veterans' graves at Monte Vista Cemetery (Town News).

Groups like the U.S. Veterans MC Trinity Chapter, chartered here in 2018 on a mission of veterans helping veterans, carry that service forward all year (Town News).

The parade may be over, but there are simple ways to honor veterans today and beyond:

Veterans seeking benefits help can contact the New Mexico Department of Veterans' Services. Any veteran in crisis, or anyone worried about one, can call or text 988 and press 1 for the Veterans Crisis Line, available around the clock.

From the F-16s over the Tularosa Basin to the flags at Monte Vista Cemetery, Alamogordo lives alongside its service members every day. Today the city simply says it out loud.

To every veteran, active-duty member and military family in Alamogordo, Holloman, Tularosa and beyond: thank you for your service.

Note article by Chris Edwards, a journalist for 2nd Life Media affiliated sites. Mr Edwards is a strong advocate and supporter of the mission of the Honor Flights, the local VFW’s upgrades and its impact of support as a safe and diverse gathering place for our veterans, and supporting the mission of team Holloman and all of our area veterans.

item.title: Solar developer pitches three sites near Tularosa as neighbors press on flooding
item.description:
TULAROSA — A community solar developer told the Tularosa Planning and Zoning Commission on Tuesday that it hopes to build as many as three solar gardens in and around the village. Neighbors of one proposed site said they don't oppose solar power, but they urged officials to make sure the project doesn't worsen flooding that already damages their property.

SunShare Community Solar has filed special use permit applications for all three sites. The company says it built its first project in Colorado Springs in 2011. It now reports more than 220 megawatts developed, about 19,000 subscribers and operations in nine states.

"We're really excited to talk to you guys about three community solar gardens that we are proposing within the village of Tularosa," said Mike, an associate developer with the company. He presented with Keenan, SunShare's director of development for New Mexico.

Under New Mexico's Community Solar Act, passed in 2021, residents and small businesses can subscribe to a solar garden and receive credits on their PNM bills. SunShare said standard subscribers save 10%.

State rules require at least 30% of each project's output to go to low-income subscribers, at a discount of at least 20%. SunShare said its projects typically reserve 50% for low-income households and give them a 30% discount. New Mexico lets residents self-attest to low-income status.

Each project would be about 5 megawatts, enough for roughly 400 to 500 subscribers, according to the company. Signing up and opting out are free. The power would flow to PNM's Tularosa substation and be used locally.

Two sites sit off Moon Valley Road. The first, which SunShare calls the Cumbre project, lies next to an existing solar array built by a different company. A smaller parcel lies to its northeast. The third site is on the north side of town off Twelfth Street, with the railroad along its west edge.

SunShare said it bought one property and is leasing the other two. Leases run 20 years with optional five-year extensions, and each site needs about 30 acres. State rules require projects to be within a mile of a three-phase power line, which representatives said explains why the sites are close to homes.

The company described sites with an 8-foot, wildlife-friendly security fence, no lighting and no batteries. It said inverters run about 58 decibels and can't be heard beyond roughly 150 feet. SunShare said it would replant native vegetation, use no chemical herbicides and post a bond to cover eventual decommissioning.

Ann Farmer, who lives on Highway 54/70 just south of the proposed Moon Valley sites, told commissioners she has no complaint about solar panels themselves.

"I have no problem with the solar field itself because I've already got one across from me," Farmer said. "They're good neighbors. They're quiet. They don't block my view."

Her concern is drainage. Farmer said flooding from a nearby arroyo has gotten worse every year since a pellet plant built a bridge over it. The last storm washed out her driveway and reached the highway, partly closing the road into town, she said. Sediment has now built up higher than her land, and her family keeps having to raise the berm that protects her house.

"The good news is we don't have that much rain, but when it comes, it just about wipes me out," she said. She said a culvert near her neighbor's driveway stays clogged. When the state tried to clean it out, it left deep ruts, she said, and she got no reply after emailing photos to the highway department.

Rick Robbins, a 75-year-old retired military veteran who has lived on Moon Valley Road for 30 years, raised the same flooding concern. "It doesn't even have to rain here in Tularosa," he said. "If it rains on the mountain over there, it funnels down and comes across Moon Valley Road."

Robbins asked who would maintain the private road that construction crews would use. He also asked whether the panels would raise nearby temperatures, citing research he found that put the increase as high as 6 degrees. He also asked about snakes and wildlife, future expansion and property values.

SunShare representatives said they had already spoken with the landowner about the arroyo. They offered to add regular ditch cleanouts to the site's maintenance contract.

"There has never been, I guess, an actual agreement in place for someone to actually do that," one representative said. "I think this is an opportunity for us to actually address it." The company also noted that a stormwater management plan is required before it can get a building permit.

On roads, SunShare said it would sign a road use agreement, post a bond if the village requires one and repair any damage. On heat, representatives said studies of the "heat island effect" show solar arrays are not a significant concern. They said panels on single-axis trackers move through the day and trap far less heat than a parking lot.

The company said program rules allow only one project per parcel, which limits expansion. On property values, a representative said studies have found effects in both directions. SunShare said glare studies for all three sites found no impacts, and early environmental and cultural reviews came back favorable.

The commission took no vote Tuesday. For special use permits, the commission doesn't approve or deny. It sends findings of fact and conditional recommendations to the Village Council, which makes the decision. Commissioners said SunShare would get a copy of their findings.

Any approval would also depend on a state contest. The projects are competing in Phase 2 of the community solar program, a competitive request for proposals run by the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission. SunShare expects bidding to open in January or February. Awards are expected around June 2027.

"Maybe we are able to get one project or two projects, maybe all three, or maybe none," Keenan said. SunShare confirmed it cannot build without a state award. If it wins, construction would likely start in early 2028 and take about three months.

Commissioners raised possible conditions, including a list of native plants, a decommissioning bond that rises each year with inflation, and an access easement for the village in case it annexes the areas, which are now in its extraterritorial jurisdiction. SunShare said it was open to each.

Opportunity zone. The commission heard that Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham has nominated three Otero County census tracts for federal opportunity zone designation, one of them in Tularosa. The others cover Alamogordo's downtown and the corridor along the Charlie Lee Memorial Relief Route. The designation would give investors federal tax breaks for putting money into those areas from 2027 through 2036. Commissioners said federal approval is usually routine. They stressed that the village needs updated ordinances in place before investors arrive: vacant building registration, then development impact fees, then a historic preservation plan.

State permit dispute. The commission approved the permit for a completed re-roof at 710 First Street. The state Construction Industries Division had issued its own permit without going through the village. Village staff said they have written to all three CID offices and are following up by phone. The homeowner paid the village fee after the work was done.

Code enforcement. Commissioners can now issue a first-notice form for planning and zoning violations, created by the village's code enforcement officer, who will handle follow-up. Residents with complaints can call the police non-emergency line. The village's ordinances can be searched on its website.

New member. The commission welcomed new member Efren Gonzalez.

The meeting adjourned at 6:50 p.m.

item.title: Tigers Get Hometown Send-Off Before 5A Quarterfinal at Los Lunas
item.description:
Alamogordo N.M. - The Alamogordo Tigers are hitting the road for the biggest game of their season, and the town is being asked to give them a proper goodbye.

Alamogordo High School will hold a Tiger Football Playoff Send-Off at 2 p.m. Friday, Nov. 13, as the team departs for Saturday's Class 5A state quarterfinal against Los Lunas. Organizers are calling on students, families, alumni, local businesses and the wider community to turn out in black and gold.

Fans who can't make it to the school are encouraged to find a spot anywhere along the route to cheer the bus as it passes.

It's a Tigers-vs.-Tigers matchup. Fifth-seeded Alamogordo (7-4) earned the trip with a dominant 54-0 first-round shutout of district rival Chaparral last Friday, its fifth straight win. Over that five-game streak, Alamogordo's defense has given up just 47 points combined — fewer than it allowed in its season opener alone.

The offense was balanced against Chaparral. Junior quarterback Nathaniel Cereceres threw for 141 yards and two touchdowns and ran for 69 yards and another score on just seven carries. Junior receiver Tristan Bowman piled up 111 receiving yards, including a 76-yard catch, and scored both through the air and on the ground. Sophomore running back Qymani Patterson added 110 rushing yards and a touchdown, breaking off a 45-yard run.

Los Lunas (7-3) is in its first season in Class 5A after moving down from 6A and earned the No. 4 seed and a first-round bye under first-year head coach Stephen Johnston. The hosts are rolling too: they closed the regular season with a 50-0 rout of Highland, and quarterback Luke Cieremans threw four touchdown passes in that game. Los Lunas' defense has allowed only 33 points over its last seven games.

First-round results (Nov. 6–7)

Roswell, Piedra Vista, Artesia and Los Lunas had first-round byes as the top four seeds.

Quarterfinals (Nov. 13–14)

What's next: Semifinals are Nov. 20–21, and the Class 5A state championship is Nov. 28 at a finalist's home site. A win Saturday would put Alamogordo in the final four.

Other quarterfinals this weekend include Class 6A's No. 1 Cleveland hosting No. 9 Rio Rancho and No. 2 Volcano Vista hosting No. 7 Carlsbad; Class 4A's No. 1 Bloomfield hosting No. 8 Valencia; and Class 3A's No. 1 St. Michael's hosting No. 8 Pojoaque Valley. Six-man crowns its champion Nov. 14, eight-man on Nov. 21, and Classes 2A through 6A on Nov. 28.

All times Mountain. Records and statistics as reported by MaxPreps

item.title: In Memory of Juan Lucio Maes
item.description:
Juan Lucio Maes, of Tularosa, New Mexico, was born on January 19, 1948, and passed away on November 4, 2026. He proudly served in the United States Army and worked for 30 years in heating and cooling (HVAC) at Holloman Air Force Base.

Juan loved his family, music, and the Tularosa Wildcats. He coached little league baseball and soccer, and enjoyed hunting, camping, and fishing.

Juan deeply loved St. Francis de Paula Catholic Church and served there in many ways over the years. He participated as a Danzante, served as a Mayordomo, and was a member of the church committee. He helped organize and manage the annual fiestas, and each Christmas he organized the church’s Luminarias. Music, hot chocolate, and cookies brought the community together for the celebration. Juan’s generosity reached beyond the church as well helping anyone he could.

Juan is survived by his wife, Virginia Maes; his daughters, Helen Butler, Jessica Iverson, Brenda Maes; his sons-in-law, Christopher Butler, Robert Iverson, Calvin Lapaz. He also leaves eight grandchildren: Brendan Chavez, Kirsten Chavez, Logan Chavez, Raven Iverson, Abram Iverson, Job Maes, Theron La Paz, Genesis La Paz; three great grandchildren: Cayson Chavez, Easton Dorame, Cayden Dorame.

Pallbearers include Joe Provencio, Brendan Chavez, Logan Chavez, Robert Iverson, Abram Iverson, Calvin Lapaz, Job Maes, Theron La Paz.

Honorary pallbearers are Christopher Butler, Mark Chino, Anthony Fresques, Joyce Amaya, Janette Mata, Robert and Cynthia Maes, Gloria Sedillo, Rayburn Chico, Michael Coyazo, Benjamin Coyazo, Paul Rocha.

Services will take place at St. Francis de Paula Catholic Church in Tularosa, New Mexico on Thursday, November 12, 2026. Viewing will be held from 9:00 am to 10:00 am. Rosary will be recited at 10:00 am with Mass celebrated at 10:30 am. Juan will be laid to rest following services at Sacred Heart Cemetery in Tularosa.

Juan will be remembered for his service, faith, and the love and generosity he shared with his family and community.

item.title: In Memory of Norman Lane
item.description:
Norman Lane, 93, passed away peacefully on September 6, 2026, in Las Cruces, New Mexico. Born and raised in Cloudcroft, New Mexico, he later made Alamogordo his home for 68 years, eventually moving to Las Cruces, NM for health care.

Norman proudly served in the United States Navy during the Korean War. After his military service, he built a successful career as a businessman and land developer. His ventures included Lane Plumbing Co., inc. in 1962, Lane Good Housekeeping Store, Desert Hills Subdivision and many others. He gave generously of his time to the community through his involvement with the Noon Lions Club, the Masonic Lodge, and the Elks Lodge. He was also a longtime member of Grace United Methodist Church.

Norman is survived by his three children, Gary Lane (Wanda), Cheri Rabon (Randy), Debbie Moore; his seven grandchildren, Kayla Lane, Norman Jaret Lane (Katie), Kelsey Joy Lane, Kristy Alsleben (Matt), Chad Rabon (Paige), Cody Lane Craig (Nikki), Abe Moore (Juliett), Josh Moore (Christine); his 14 great grandchildren.

Family was at the heart of Norman's life. He was preceded in death by Joy, the love of his life. Together, they shared 69 wonderful years of marriage. He was also preceded in death by his parents, Les and Jennie Lane; his brothers, Rex "Buster" Lane, Gene Lane, Dutch Lane; his son-in-law, Doug Moore; his grandson, Eli Moore.

He leaves behind many special friends including his dear friend, Yvonne Brown, as well as countless lives he touched over the years.

Those who knew Norman will remember his strong work ethic, outgoing spirit, and love of life. He never met a stranger and enjoyed connecting with people wherever he went. He loved classic cars, traveling in his RV, watching sports, and spending many years making memories at Elephant Butte lake.

More than anything, Norman's greatest legacy was his family. He will be deeply missed and lovingly remembered by his children, grandchildren, great grandchildren, extended family, and many friends. He often told anyone who would listen how blessed he was and how grateful he felt to have lived 93 full and meaningful years.

A Celebration of Life will be held for Norman from 1:00 pm to 3:00 pm on Monday, November 23, 2026, at the Elks Lodge located at 2290 Hamilton Road in Alamogordo.
